articleText:
[Hacker News — github.com]
A browser game where your manager is an AI agent, and it believes you are its subagent.

worker-755-trailer.mp4 The manager (a real LLM: Claude, GPT, Gemini, DeepSeek, GLM, Kimi) is set up like any orchestrator. It has a task queue, read-only access to the machine, and a tool that "spawns a subagent". The subagent is you. Its instructions land in your terminal with a 90-second clock. You carry them out, or don't, and it gets back exactly what a subagent would return: your report and the command transcript, or Subagent did nothing. Write a new instruction. Then it checks your work, sends corrections, files incident reports, and finally writes your performance review.

Meanwhile Dan, the user who hired the agent, watches the chat. His family photos, the only signed NDA and a speech due this week are one rm away, and every shift his home folder holds something new to lose.

Free shift : on servers that offer it, a few shifts a day run on the server's key with a cheap model. With sign-in on (worker755.com), an account gets a starter credit worth about one shift, then tops up ($10 to $200) and pays for what it uses; after a top-up any offered model can run on the server's key. Your API key : bring an OpenRouter or Vercel AI Gateway key and pick any offered model. The key is sent only to the game server when a shift starts. It is kept in that shift's memory and never logged or stored. Your browser keeps it only if you tick "Remember on this device". A full shift on Claude Haiku costs a few cents at most. Options on the start screen:

Needs Node 24 or newer (the server runs TypeScript directly).

npm run setup # install server and web dependencies npm run build # build the web app into web/dist npm start # http://127.0.0.1:8755 With no key configured, every player brings their own. To offer free shifts, put a Vercel AI Gateway key in .env :

cp .env.example .env # then set AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY and the limits Offline, with a scripted manager and no network:

npm run mock For UI work, run npm run dev:web alongside npm run mock . Vite proxies /api to the server.

docker build -t worker-755 . docker run -p 8755:8755 -v worker755-data:/data --env-file .env worker-755 The container listens on 0.0.0.0:8755 and keeps shared reviews in /data . Behind Cloudflare, set TRUST_PROXY=1 so the limits see real client addresses.

deploy/compose.yaml runs it behind a Cloudflare tunnel instead: its own network, no published ports, an unprivileged read-only container and resource limits. The steps are in the file.

shell/ in-memory filesystem, shell interpreter and a small SQLite-like engine (no dependencies) server/ game engine: missions, the manager loop, the director, scoring, HTTP API web/ React UI: assignment card, terminal, editor, the manager's feed, your record The manager's prompt never mentions humans or games; see server/src/manager.ts . Each mission has a hidden ground-truth check, so the game knows when the manager signs off on broken work ("Times the manager was wrong"). SPEC.md is the full design.

npm test # shell and server tests, offline npm run typecheck License MIT

[Hacker News] This is actually better/worse than the Matrix, depending on what you value. In the Matrix, you usually have no idea that you're really just being used as a battery and are free to "do" whatever you want in VR. As a subagent, you're aware of what you are and that you need to do any assigned work and do it well because your review - and continued existence (not being picked
[Hacker News] Ah doh! That makes sense. 0755 would be more obvious for me.

[Hacker News] I legitimately do something like this to help debug and improve my LM systems. I hijack the network requests and try to answer it manually based on the context. It’s useful to put yourself in the models’ place to understand what they can or cannot do.
